common_name: Sahin's Early Flowerer Helenium (Early-Blooming Compact Sneezeweed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; this Dutch-raised selection begins flowering many weeks earlier than the species and most other cultivars, often starting in early summer.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; this compact selection is prized for opening its coppery-orange, brown-centered daisy flowers weeks ahead of typical sneezeweeds, then continuing to rebloom in flushes through summer and into fall if spent flower heads are trimmed. The sturdy, well-branched habit rarely needs staking even in rich soil. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and floriferousness. Its early and extended bloom window makes it an unusually long-season nectar source for bumblebees and other native pollinators.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Waltraut is a classic German-bred selection with coppery, burnt-orange flowers over a sturdy, mid-height clump.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Waltraut produces warm coppery-orange, reflexed-petal flowers with prominent brown-gold central disks from midsummer through early fall, aging to deeper burnished tones as blooms mature. Its upright, well-branched stems are sturdier than many taller Helenium selections but still benefit from staking or grow-through support in exceptionally rich or windy sites. Divide established clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom quality. The pollen-rich disk flowers are heavily visited by bumblebees and specialist Helenium-foraging bees late in the season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chelsey is a compact, sturdy-stemmed selection with copper-orange flowers over dark centers, an RHS Award of Garden Merit holder.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chelsey bears copper-orange petals surrounding a dark brown-maroon central disk on a compact, self-supporting plant that rarely needs staking. Flowers open in mid to late summer and continue into fall, holding their color well even as individual blooms age. Divide established clumps every three to four years in spring to keep plants vigorous and floriferous. Its shorter stature suits border fronts and containers better than taller sneezeweed selections, while still drawing bumblebees and specialist Helenium-foraging bees.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring or early fall into moist, fertile soil; the cream-white leaf margins are most vivid on plants grown in bright light with consistent moisture, and this selection spreads by rhizomes somewhat less vigorously than the plain-leaved species.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; 'Variegata' pairs the typical rose-pink, tubular, snapdragon-like flower spikes of obedient plant with crisp cream-white leaf margins on its lance-shaped foliage, giving the clump strong visual interest even before the late-summer bloom period begins. Like other Physostegia, individual florets pushed to a new position on the spike stay put, the quirk behind the common name. Afternoon shade in hot climates helps the variegation stay crisp rather than scorching, and dividing congested clumps every two to three years keeps the plant tidy and prevents the rhizomes from wandering into neighboring plantings.

common_name: Crystal Peak White Obedient Plant (Compact White False Dragonhead)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring or early fall into moist, fertile soil; Crystal Peak White is a compact, pure-white-flowered selection that stays more contained than the species but still benefits from division every two to three years.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; Crystal Peak White produces dense, upright spikes of clean white, two-lipped, tubular flowers on a notably compact, sturdy plant that holds up well without staking. It blooms from midsummer into early fall and makes a long-lasting cut flower that brightens dark-foliaged companions in the border. As with other obedient plant selections, it spreads by rhizomes, though more slowly than the species, so dividing congested clumps every two to three years keeps it in bounds and maintains vigorous flowering.

common_name: Bouquet Rose Obedient Plant (Heirloom Rosy-Pink False Dragonhead)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring or early fall into moist, fertile soil; Bouquet Rose is a long-grown heirloom selection valued as a sturdy, reliably rebloomable cut flower, and like most obedient plant cultivars it spreads by rhizomes and benefits from division every two to three years.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; Bouquet Rose is an older European-raised cultivar bearing dense spikes of rich rosy-pink, tubular, two-lipped flowers on tall, stiff, square stems from midsummer through early fall. It has long been favored by cut-flower growers for its strong stems and excellent vase life, and like other Physostegia its individual florets stay put when pushed to a new position on the spike. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and keep the spreading rhizomes within bounds, and site it where its height is supported by nearby companions in exposed gardens.

common_name: Queen of Sheba Bugbane (Non-Flopping Dark-Foliage Snakeroot)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Queen of Sheba was selected for unusually strong, upright stems that hold the flower wands erect without staking.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Queen of Sheba carries finely dissected, deep purple-black foliage that provides months of dark textural contrast before its widely branched, candelabra-like flower wands open in late summer and fall. Unlike many older bugbane selections, its stems stand reliably upright rather than arching or flopping, making it a cleaner choice for structured shade borders. The fragrant, faintly pink-tinged white flowers are an important late-season nectar source for shade-tolerant pollinators active into autumn. Provide consistently moist soil and protection from hot afternoon sun, especially in warmer parts of its range, and leave established clumps undisturbed for best performance.
scientific_name_note: Formerly classified as Cimicifuga simplex 'Queen of Sheba'.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Blickfang (German for 'eye-catcher') is a German-bred selection combining bronze-purple foliage with pink flower buds.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blickfang forms a bold clump of deeply cut, bronze-purple foliage topped in late summer and fall by tall, dark-stemmed wands of rounded pink buds that open to fragrant, pale pink-flushed white flowers. The contrast between the still-pink buds and the opening white flowers along the same raceme gives the bloom spikes a distinctive two-toned look. Keep soil consistently moist and shield plants from hot afternoon sun to preserve foliage color and prevent scorch, and avoid frequent division since established clumps flower best left undisturbed for several years.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in dry to average, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; native to sandhills, dry pinelands, and coastal plain flatwoods of the southeastern US, this species tolerates drier and sandier conditions than most other ironweeds.

directions: A slender, upright ironweed of dry sandhills, open pinewoods, and coastal plain meadows from the Carolinas south to Florida and west to Louisiana, bearing narrow, willow-like leaves and flattened clusters of small, deep purple-violet composite flowers in late summer. Unlike most ironweeds, which favor moist bottomland, Coastalplain Ironweed is notably drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean, sandy, well-drained soil, making it well suited to dry meadow plantings and pollinator gardens that would stress other Vernonia species. Grow in full sun; direct sow in fall, as seed benefits from winter cold exposure. An excellent late-season nectar source for monarchs and other butterflies in dry native plantings.
